Many insects, such as butterflies and moths, but also most bugs do not hatch from their eggs in a complete adult form, but rather begin life in a larval state (caterpillars and maggots, for instance) which only later on undergoes metamorphosis into an adult form of their respective species.

I'm curious as to why this mechanism has evolved in those animal - in most of them, the larval stage is slower and more vulnerable towards predators than the adult form, doubly so in species who go fully immobile during their metamorphosis as the larva turns into a pupa. At the same time, at least some insect such as grasshoppers seem to be capable of hatching fully developed as far as their physical appearance is concerned, and simply grow into fully-sized adult animals over several moulting phases.

So, why bother with the larval and pupa stage? At best I could imagine that some species can not store enough nutrients in their eggs to fuel an internal transformation of the embryo inside into its (small) adult form, so the half-developed embryo hatches early, consumes food to store nutrients, and later finishes this process, but even so, the increased vulnerability during the larval and pupa stage may offset this.

Or, may it alternatively be the case that the pupation mechanism actually is older than that of embryos hatching in their finished adult form?
